lead: This unit explains why engines have a limit. You will learn the two statements of the second law, the Carnot cycle, the thermodynamic temperature scale, the Clausius inequality and entropy, then use them to find entropy changes and to judge whether a process can happen at all.
about: This unit starts from a simple question: why does heat never flow uphill on its own? It defines heat engines, refrigerators and heat pumps with their efficiency and COP, then states the second law in its Kelvin-Planck and Clausius forms and proves them equivalent. Reversible and irreversible processes lead to the Carnot cycle and Carnot’s theorem, and the theorem gives a temperature scale tied to no substance. The Clausius inequality then defines entropy, which is read on the T-s diagram and used in the principle of increase of entropy. The entropy balance of a control volume turns that principle into numbers for real devices, together with the molecular view of entropy, and the third law closes the unit by fixing the zero of entropy.

chapters.idea: A heat engine takes heat from a hot reservoir, turns part of it into work and dumps the rest; a refrigerator or heat pump runs the same device backwards and pays for it with work.
chapters.depth: Define thermal reservoir, source and sink, then heat engine, refrigerator and heat pump as the same three parts: a hot reservoir at T₁, a cold reservoir at T₂, and a cyclic device between them. For an engine, Q₁ = W + Q₂ and η = W/Q₁. For reversed devices, COP_R = Q₂/W and COP_HP = Q₁/W, so COP_HP = COP_R + 1. State clearly that η is always below 1 while a COP is usually above 1. Note that room air conditioners are rated in tons of cooling, and 1 ton ≈ 3.517 kW, so a 1.5 ton unit removes about 5.3 kW of heat. Some syllabi call COP the performance factor. Use only the first-law energy balance here, with no second-law limit.

figure.title: Energy flow through a cyclic device
figure.aria: Heat Q₁ from a hot reservoir enters a cyclic device, which rejects Q₂ to a cold reservoir and delivers work W.

chapters.example: A cyclic engine receives 800 kJ of heat from a reservoir at 600 K and rejects 500 kJ to a reservoir at 300 K. Find the work output and the thermal efficiency. The same device is then run backwards as a refrigerator using 300 kJ of work; find its COP, and its COP when run as a heat pump.
chapters.trap: Students write η = W/Q₂, and they forget COP_HP = COP_R + 1. A COP above 1 is normal and is not a violation of energy conservation, because the COP compares heat moved with work paid, not heat with heat.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 (heat, work, sign convention) and Unit 2 (first law applied to a cycle).
chapters.leave: Whether 37.5% is the best possible is answered in 3.2 and 3.4. Real power plants, refrigerators and their circuits belong to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: The second law is stated in two equivalent ways, and each forbids a different impossible machine.
chapters.depth: Write the Kelvin-Planck statement: no cyclic device can take heat from a single reservoir and convert all of it into work. Write the Clausius statement: no device can move heat from a colder body to a hotter body with no work input and no other change. Say at once that neither statement follows from the first law and that both talk about cyclic devices. Prove equivalence both ways: use a 100% engine to drive a reversible refrigerator, and use a work-free refrigerator to build a 100% engine. Name the 100% cyclic engine a perpetual motion machine of the second kind (PMM2) and show it does not break the first law. Add the corollaries: heat flows hot to cold by itself, a cycle cannot give net work while touching one reservoir, and no real engine reaches 100%.

figure.title: How one violation creates the other
figure.aria: A 100% engine makes work with no heat rejection, the work drives a refrigerator, and the pair cools the cold reservoir with no work input and no other change.

chapters.example: An inventor claims an engine that takes 1000 kJ from a reservoir at 500 K, rejects 400 kJ to a reservoir at 300 K and delivers 600 kJ of work. Show that this claim violates the Kelvin-Planck statement, and use the excess work in a reversible refrigerator between the same two reservoirs to show that it violates the Clausius statement too.
chapters.trap: The Kelvin-Planck statement is about a cyclic device, not a single process. An isothermal expansion of an ideal gas does convert heat fully into work, and that is perfectly allowed. Also, the two statements are not two laws; they are the same law.
chapters.prereq: 3.1 for the engine and refrigerator pictures, and Unit 2 for the first-law energy balance.
chapters.leave: The numerical limit on efficiency is derived in 3.4. What makes a real machine fall short of the limit is 3.3.

chapters.idea: A process is reversible only if it can be reversed completely and leaves no trace anywhere in the system or the surroundings.
chapters.depth: Define a reversible process as quasi-static (no finite unbalanced force, no finite temperature difference) and free of all dissipative effects. Distinguish internal reversibility, which concerns gradients inside the system, from external reversibility, which concerns the system and its surroundings. List the causes of irreversibility with everyday pictures: friction in a pump, unrestrained or free expansion of gas, heat transfer across a finite temperature difference, mixing of two water streams, current through a resistance, plastic deformation of a metal. Compare reversible and irreversible processes: infinitely slow against real speed, zero gradients against finite gradients, maximum work out and minimum work in against less work out and more work in. Say plainly that a reversible process is a limit used for calculation and is never achieved exactly.

figure.aria: A smooth isothermal curve and a staircase of finite steps lie at different pressures for the same volumes, the staircase doing more work.

chapters.example: 0.5 kg of air at 300 K expands from 0.2 m³ to 0.4 m³ at constant temperature (R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K). Find the work if the expansion is reversible and isothermal. Find the work if the same gas expands freely into an evacuated flask, and state the work lost. Answer: W_rev = mRT ln(v₂/v₁) = 43.05 × 0.693 = 29.8 kJ; free expansion gives W = 0, so 29.8 kJ of work is lost.
chapters.trap: Slow is not the same as reversible. A quasi-static process with friction still creates heat inside the system and remains irreversible. Always check both conditions: no gradients and no dissipation.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 (quasi-static process, path and state) and Unit 2 (isothermal and adiabatic processes).
chapters.leave: The entropy change of an irreversible process is quantified in 3.7 and 3.8, and the lost work is priced as exergy in Unit 4.

chapters.idea: The Carnot cycle is the best possible cycle between two reservoirs, and its efficiency depends only on those two temperatures.
chapters.depth: Build the Carnot cycle from four reversible steps on a gas: isothermal expansion at T₁ taking Q₁, isentropic expansion from T₁ to T₂, isothermal compression at T₂ rejecting Q₂, and isentropic compression back to state 1. Describe its shape on the p-v diagram and its shape as a rectangle on the T-s diagram. Derive η = 1 − T₂/T₁ using Q₁ = mRT₁ ln(v₂/v₁) and Q₂ = mRT₂ ln(v₃/v₄) with v₂/v₁ = v₃/v₄. State the result holds for every working substance. Give Carnot's theorem in two parts: no engine between two fixed reservoirs is more efficient than a reversible one, and all reversible engines between the same two reservoirs have equal efficiency whatever the substance, the size of the cycle or the pressures used. Some syllabi call this Carnot's principle and list the second part as a corollary.

figure.title: Four reversible steps of the Carnot cycle
figure.aria: The cycle runs from isothermal expansion to adiabatic expansion to isothermal compression to adiabatic compression and closes back on state one.

chapters.example: 1 kg of air (R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K) runs a Carnot cycle between 900 K and 300 K. The isothermal expansion at 900 K takes the volume from 0.1 m³ to 0.2 m³. Find Q₁, Q₂, W and η. Answer: Q₁ = mRT₁ ln(v₂/v₁) = 1 × 0.287 × 900 × 0.693 = 179.0 kJ; Q₂ = Q₁T₂/T₁ = 59.7 kJ; W = 119.3 kJ; η = 1 − 300/900 = 66.7%.
chapters.trap: Temperatures must be in kelvin: 1 − T₂/T₁ with °C gives nonsense. Also the efficiency is a per-cycle ratio of energies; it does not depend on the mass of gas or on how large the cycle is.
chapters.prereq: 3.3 (reversible processes) and Unit 2 (isothermal and adiabatic work for an ideal gas).
chapters.leave: The T-s picture in full, with entropy values, is 3.7. Real cycles that try to imitate Carnot, such as Rankine and Brayton, are Unit 6.

chapters.idea: A reversible engine gives a temperature scale free of any substance, defined by T₁/T₂ = Q₁/Q₂.
chapters.depth: Start with the practical problem: gas thermometers using different gases disagree slightly, so a temperature scale must not depend on the working substance. Use Carnot's theorem: every reversible engine between the same two reservoirs has the same efficiency, so the ratio Q₁/Q₂ depends only on the two temperatures. Define the thermodynamic (Kelvin) scale by T₁/T₂ = Q₁/Q₂ and show that this makes η = 1 − T₂/T₁ exactly, for every substance. Explain that the definition fixes only ratios, so one fixed point is needed; the triple point of water is taken as 273.16 K. State that the scale coincides with the ideal-gas scale, so readings need no correction. Note that η = 100% would need T₂ = 0 K, which is not available.

figure.aria: Efficiency rises towards one as the source temperature grows, and the curve for the colder sink of 300 K lies above the curve for the 600 K sink.

chapters.example: Two reversible engines work in series. The first takes heat from a source at T₁ and rejects it at T₂; the second takes that heat at T₂ and rejects it at 300 K. Each engine has a thermal efficiency of 20%. Find T₁ and T₂ on the thermodynamic scale.
chapters.trap: The reversible engine defines only ratios of temperatures. Without one fixed point the numbers are arbitrary. Also, this scale is defined through a reversible engine, so it cannot be used to compute the efficiency of a real engine; it is the yardstick that the real engine is measured against.
chapters.prereq: 3.4 (Carnot cycle and theorem) and Unit 1 (temperature and the zeroth law).
chapters.leave: Thermometry and temperature measurement devices are Unit 1. The equality case of the inequality that this scale leads to is 3.6.

chapters.idea: For any cycle, the sum of δQ/T around the cycle is zero if the cycle is reversible and negative if it is irreversible.
chapters.depth: State the Clausius inequality as ∮δQ/T ≤ 0, with δQ taken positive when heat enters the system and T the temperature of the boundary where that heat crosses; when the heat comes from a reservoir, T is the reservoir temperature. Prove it by coupling the actual cycle to a reversible engine working with a reservoir at T₀, and show that a positive result would break the Kelvin-Planck statement. Read the three cases: equality for a reversible cycle, less than zero for an irreversible one, greater than zero impossible. Show that the Kelvin-Planck statement is the special case of a cycle with one reservoir, and say that the inequality is the seed of both entropy (3.7) and the increase of entropy (3.8).

figure.title: Reading the sign of the cyclic integral
figure.aria: A real cycle is compared with a reversible one, its cyclic integral of heat over temperature is formed, and the sign of that integral sorts the cycle into reversible, irreversible or impossible.

chapters.example: A cycle receives 500 kJ at 600 K, rejects 300 kJ at 300 K and delivers 200 kJ of work. Evaluate ∮δQ/T and decide whether the cycle is reversible, irreversible or impossible. Answer: 500/600 − 300/300 = 0.833 − 1.000 = −0.167 kJ/K, so the cycle is irreversible. Its efficiency is 200/500 = 40%, below the Carnot value of 50% for these two temperatures.
chapters.trap: Sign errors. Heat leaving must be entered with a minus sign, and the temperature must be the one at which the heat crosses the boundary, in kelvin, not the instantaneous system temperature during an internal process.
chapters.prereq: 3.4 and 3.5 for the reversible reference cycle and the temperature scale.
chapters.leave: The property that comes out of the equality case is built in 3.7; the use of the inequality to price lost work is Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Entropy is a property defined by dS = δQ_rev/T, and its change fixes the direction a process can take.
chapters.depth: Use the Clausius inequality on a pair of reversible paths to show that ∫δQ_rev/T between two states is the same for all reversible paths, so it defines a property. Write dS = δQ_rev/T with units kJ/K or kJ/kg·K, and S as an extensive property. Read a T-s diagram: for a reversible process Q = ∫T dS, so the area under the path is the heat, and the Carnot cycle appears as a rectangle. Give the ideal-gas relations ΔS = m[cv ln(T₂/T₁) + R ln(v₂/v₁)] and ΔS = m[cp ln(T₂/T₁) − R ln(p₂/p₁)], then the special cases: isothermal ΔS = mR ln(v₂/v₁), isobaric ΔS = m cp ln(T₂/T₁), isochoric ΔS = m cv ln(T₂/T₁), isentropic ΔS = 0. Note that a constant-pressure curve on the T-s diagram has slope T/cp and a constant-volume curve has slope T/cv, so the constant-volume curve is steeper. Some syllabi list this as entropy change in non-flow processes and entropy of a perfect gas.

figure.aria: Both curves start at 300 K and rise with entropy, and the constant-volume curve climbs more steeply than the constant-pressure curve.

chapters.example: 2 kg of air is heated at constant pressure from 300 K to 600 K. Find the entropy change (cp = 1.005 kJ/kg·K, cv = 0.718 kJ/kg·K, R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K). Answer: ΔS = m cp ln(T₂/T₁) = 2 × 1.005 × 0.693 = 1.393 kJ/K. Check with the other form: this is the same as a constant-volume heating from 300 K to 600 K plus an isothermal expansion, giving m cv ln 2 + mR ln 2 = 2 × 0.718 × 0.693 + 2 × 0.287 × 0.693 = 0.995 + 0.398 = 1.393 kJ/K.
chapters.trap: Entropy is a property, so ΔS depends only on the end states; never integrate δQ/T along an irreversible path. Use cp at constant pressure and cv at constant volume, and always put T in kelvin.
chapters.prereq: 3.6 (Clausius inequality) and Unit 2 (ideal-gas processes and specific heats).
chapters.leave: The entropy of steam and the use of steam tables are Unit 5. Absolute values of entropy from the third law are 3.9.

chapters.idea: The total entropy of a system and its surroundings never decreases, and every real process creates entropy.
chapters.depth: State the principle as ΔS_system + ΔS_surroundings = S_gen ≥ 0, with S_gen in kJ/K, and note that the equality holds only for a reversible process. Give the second law in entropy words: the entropy of an isolated system increases in every real process. Explain S_gen as a quantitative measure of irreversibility, larger for a bigger temperature gap, more friction or more mixing, and zero for a reversible adiabatic process, which is isentropic. Show the four standard sources of S_gen: heat through a finite temperature difference, mixing of two streams, unrestrained expansion and friction. Add one line that the same inequality gives a criterion for spontaneous change (dS ≥ 0 at constant internal energy and volume) and that only a few universities ask for this form. Point to Unit 4 for lost work and exergy.

figure.title: Entropy created when heat crosses a temperature gap
figure.aria: One hundred kilojoules flows from a 500 K body to a 300 K body, the hot body loses 0.200 kJ/K of entropy and the cold body gains 0.333 kJ/K, leaving a net creation of 0.133 kJ/K.

chapters.example: 2 kg of water at 80 °C is mixed with 3 kg of water at 20 °C in an insulated vessel (cp = 4.187 kJ/kg·K). Find the final temperature and the total entropy change. Answer: T_f = (2 × 353 + 3 × 293)/5 = 317 K = 44 °C. ΔS = 2 × 4.187 × ln(317/353) + 3 × 4.187 × ln(317/293) = −0.901 + 0.989 = +0.088 kJ/K, which is positive, so the mixing is irreversible and possible.
chapters.trap: The entropy of the system alone may fall: water freezing and gas compressing both do it. Only system plus surroundings is guaranteed to be non-negative. Also, a positive ΔS says the process can happen, not that it happens quickly.
chapters.prereq: 3.7 (entropy and its changes) and 3.3 (causes of irreversibility).
chapters.leave: Available and unavailable energy, second law efficiency and exergy analysis are Unit 4. The Carnot limit used for comparison is 3.4.

chapters.idea: Entropy balance for closed systems and control volumes, entropy generation, lost work, and S = k ln W.
At absolute zero the entropy of a perfect crystal is zero, and absolute zero itself cannot be reached in a finite number of steps.
chapters.depth: State the Nernst heat theorem and the third law: for a perfectly ordered crystal at equilibrium, S → 0 as T → 0 K, so entropy can be measured on an absolute scale instead of only as a difference. Give S(T) = ∫₀ᵀ (cp/T) dT and explain that below the lowest measured temperature the Debye T³ law, cp = aT³, is used to complete the integral. Show why the classical expression S = cp ln T fails: it runs to minus infinity as T falls to zero. State the unattainability of absolute zero: each step of adiabatic demagnetisation cools the sample a little, but a finite number of steps never reaches 0 K. Add the consequence cp → 0 as T → 0. Say that only a few universities ask for numerical absolute entropies; most ask for the statement and the unattainability argument.

figure.aria: The real entropy curve starts at zero and flattens near absolute zero, while the classical logarithmic curve dives to large negative values as temperature falls.

chapters.example: A solid follows the Debye law below 10 K with cp = aT³, where a = 0.002 J/(mol·K⁴). Taking S = 0 at 0 K, find the entropy at 10 K. Answer: S = ∫₀¹⁰ (aT³/T) dT = aT² dT integrated = aT³/3 = 0.002 × 1000/3 = 0.667 J/(mol·K).
chapters.trap: Zero entropy at 0 K applies to a perfect crystal at equilibrium. Glasses, solid solutions and crystals with frozen-in defects keep a residual entropy. Also, absolute zero is unattainable, not merely hard to reach.
chapters.prereq: 3.7 (entropy as a property) and 3.8 (entropy as a state function of the whole system).
chapters.leave: The integration of real cp data over a full temperature range, and the steam tables that carry absolute entropy values for water, are Unit 5.
